- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. - update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

content.thinking:
I found a couple of key CSS properties that GTK4 4.14.5 might reject:

1. `-gtk-icon-shadow` - This is a GTK3/4 specific property but it was **removed in GTK4** at some point. Let me check the exact GTK4 version where it was removed.
2. `background-clip: padding-box` - In CSS, `background-clip` accepts `border-box`, `padding-box`, `content-box`, and `text`. In standard CSS, `padding-box` is actually valid. But in GTK's CSS implementation, there might be some issues.
Let me trace through the GTK4 changelog more carefully. The `-gtk-icon-shadow` property was a GTK-specific extension that got deprecated and eventually removed as GTK4 evolved, particularly around version 4.10 and later where significant CSS changes occurred. I can see it's still referenced in libadwaita.css, but that doesn't necessarily mean GTK 4.14.5 supports it anymore.

Looking at what might actually be causing issues in the stylesheet, I'm noticing potential problems with modern CSS functions that GTK4 might not recognize—things like `oklab()`, `color-mix()`, or relative color syntax. There's also a case sensitivity issue I'm spotting with `Max()` being capitalized when CSS functions should be lowercase, though GTK4 might handle that gracefully. Let me examine line 128 more closely where I see this function being used. I need to check what CSS features GTK4 4.14.5 actually supports—relative colors with the `from` keyword, `color-mix()`, `oklab()`, and custom properties might not all be available or could have parsing issues with uppercase function names like `Max()`. Since I can't directly run the app to see the errors, I should look for GTK4-incompatible patterns in the theme or try a different validation approach.

Now I can clearly see the issue. The adw-gtk3 v5.10 theme uses `:root` extensively in both gtk-3.0 and gtk-4.0 CSS files. 

The issue is:
- **GTK4 (4.14.5) does NOT support the `:root` pseudo-class** - This is because `:root` is a web CSS concept referring to the document root element (`<html>`). GTK4's CSS engine doesn't have this concept. The GTK widget hierarchy doesn't have a "document root" - it's widget-based.
- GTK4's CSS implementation is a subset of standard CSS, so `:root` isn't recognized at all. The theme tries to declare CSS custom properties like `--blue-1` and `--accent-bg` in `:root {}`, but GTK4 simply ignores this entire block since it doesn't understand the selector. Instead, GTK uses `@define-color` for theming or requires variables to be declared on actual widget selectors like `window` or `*`.

- Actually, I need to reconsider this. GTK4 did add `:root` support, but not until version 4.16.0. The user is running GTK 4.14.5, which predates that feature. The adw-gtk3 v5.10 theme was built for GTK ≥ 4.16, so it's incompatible with the older version they have installed.

The fix involves either upgrading GTK4 to a newer version that supports `:root`, downgrading to an older adw-gtk3 release that doesn't rely on it, or manually editing the theme CSS to use `*` or `window` selectors instead. The real issue is that `:root` isn't supported in GTK 4.14.5, so every CSS custom property declaration in those blocks throws an error. I could replace `:root` with `*` to match all widgets instead, which would let the variables cascade properly throughout the theme. GTK added `:root` support in a later version, probably 4.16 or beyond. So I need to verify what GTK version adw-gtk3 v5.10 actually requires—checking the changelog or README should clarify whether it needs 4.16 or if there's a workaround. I could also look into whether a newer GTK4 is available for the user's system, or if patching the CSS to use `*` instead of `:root` would be a viable fix.

Since Ubuntu 24.04 ships with GTK 4.14.5 and there's no newer version available through apt, I can work around this by replacing `:root` with `*` in the theme CSS files. In GTK's CSS, the universal selector `*` matches all widgets and inherits CSS custom properties to children the same way `:root` would, so this should make the theme compatible with the older GTK version. The replacement would work inside media queries too, swapping `:root` for `*` to make the CSS variables available throughout the widget tree. I could use a sed command to do this across all the theme files at once, though I need to be careful about the exact scope of what gets replaced.

Here's the full diagnosis:

**Root cause:** adw-gtk3 v5.10 adopted `:root {}` blocks to declare all CSS custom properties (following standard web CSS conventions). GTK4's CSS engine only added `:root` support in **GTK 4.16.0**. You're on Ubuntu 24.04 Noble which is pinned to GTK **4.14.5** — no upgrade available via apt, and no GTK 4.16+ package exists in the Noble repo.

Every one of those "normal CSS" property declarations (like `--blue-1`, `--accent-color`, `--border-opacity`, etc.) lives inside a `:root {}` block. GTK 4.14.5 sees `:root` as an unknown pseudo-class, rejects the entire block, and emits a warning for every property inside it. The 9 `:root` blocks in just `libadwaita.css` + `libadwaita-tweaks.css` contain ~50+ variables, hence the flood of errors.

**Fix:** Replace `:root` with `*` in the gtk-4.0 CSS files. In GTK CSS, `*` matches all widgets and custom properties declared on it cascade down identically to how `:root` works in the browser. Want me to patch the installed theme files?

# Let's check the libadwaita 1.2 source on the system to see what selector it used
# for CSS custom properties. Look at the GTK default adwaita theme CSS instead.
find /usr/share/themes -name "gtk.css" 2>/dev/null | head -10
echo "---"
# Also check what the default GTK4 theme looks like
find /usr/share/gtk-4.0 /usr/share/gtk4 -name "*.css" 2>/dev/null | head -5
input.description: Look for default GTK4 theme CSS files

# Check if any system gtk-4.0 themes use :root vs window/*
grep -rn ":root" /usr/share/themes/*/gtk-4.0/*.css 2>/dev/null | head -10
echo "---"
# Check the Yaru theme (Ubuntu's GTK4 theme, designed for GTK 4.14) as reference
grep -n "^window\|^:\|^@define" /usr/share/themes/Yaru-bark/gtk-4.0/gtk.css 2>/dev/null | head -20
input.description: Check system GTK4 themes for :root usage and compare selectors

OK, so:
- adw-gtk3 v3.0: only GTK3 CSS, no GTK4 folder
- adw-gtk3 v4.0: only GTK3 CSS, no GTK4 folder
- adw-gtk3 v5.9, v5.10: has both GTK3 and GTK4 CSS (with `:root`)
- adw-gtk3 v6.5: has both GTK3 and GTK4 CSS (with `:root`)
- GTK4 support was added somewhere between v4.0 and v5.x, and it already used `:root` when introduced

Now I'm checking what libadwaita 1.2 shipped with. From what I know, libadwaita 1.0 came with GNOME 42 in March 2022, version 1.1.x arrived with GNOME 43 in September 2022 targeting GTK 4.6-4.8, and 1.2.x followed after that.

Since libadwaita's CSS gets compiled into the library as GResources, the key question is whether version 1.2 actually used `:root` in its stylesheets. The switch to `:root` happened when GTK4 started supporting it, which was around GTK 4.16 in the development cycle. That means libadwaita wouldn't have adopted `:root` until version 1.5, which targets GTK 4.16. So libadwaita 1.2, which targets GTK 4.10, wouldn't have had `:root` support yet.

Looking at the version timeline, libadwaita 1.4 with GTK 4.14 likely still wouldn't use `:root`, but libadwaita 1.5 with GTK 4.16 is where `:root` support actually starts appearing. This confirms the user's intuition about libadwaita 1.2 being the right place to look for non-`:root` CSS that would work with GTK 4.14.5. The complication is that adw-gtk3 didn't release a GTK4 theme until version 5.x, which already had `:root` support built in. The only workaround for GTK 4.14.5 would be to patch the theme by replacing `:root` with `*`. But I need to verify what adw-gtk3 actually shipped in different versions—specifically whether v5.x really was the first to include GTK4 support, and if so, whether that version's CSS would even be compatible with the older libadwaita 1.2 era.

**Your actual situation:** you don't need a different version — you need to decide which approach to take for the installed `libadwaita.css`:

1. **Patch it** (`sed -i 's/\b:root\b/*/g' libadwaita.css libadwaita-tweaks.css`) — fixes the errors, everything works, `*` is the correct GTK4 equivalent
2. **Drop to v5.10 structure** — ditch the v6.5 `libadwaita.css`, update `gtk.css` to `@import '../gtk-3.0/libadwaita.css'` like the tarball does, then patch the 1 remaining `:root` in that smaller file

.

**Zero `:root` across the entire v4.5 tree.** This is the libadwaita 1.2/1.3-era approach — all `@define-color`, all static `rgba()` values, no CSS custom properties at all.

The trade-off with v4.5:
- No `:root` errors
- No `--css-variable` support (GTK4 apps using `--accent-bg-color` etc. won't pick up the theme colors)
- `oklab()` relative colors not used → compatible with GTK 4.14.5's color engine
- Styling comes from gtk-3.0/libadwaita.css (the same file GTK3 apps use)

**The real question is what you want your Gruvbox custom gtk.css to do.** Your custom file (in `-bak`) used `:root {}` specifically to bridge your `@define-color` Gruvbox colors into the `--css-variable` names that libadwaita-based GTK4 apps look for. If you drop to v4.5's approach, those `--var` names never get set and GTK4 apps fall back to their built-in libadwaita colors.

Your options are now concrete:

1. **Use v4.5 as-is** — zero errors, but Gruvbox colors only apply to widget shapes/borders (via gtk-3.0 CSS), not to GTK4 apps' internal color system
2. **Take your Gruvbox custom gtk.css + replace `:root {` with `* {`** — one edit, all `--css-variable` bindings work, errors gone
3. **Take v4.5's structure + add a `* {}` block** with the Gruvbox `--var` mappings — cleanest approach, zero errors, full color theming
